Abstract
Existing Large Language Model-driven automated unit test generation methods
still have limitations in test intent understanding, contextual information organiza-
tion, and generated-result validation, making it difficult to steadily improve the
quality and coverage of generated test code. To address this problem, this paper
proposes an automated unit test generation method based on iterative optimization
with dynamic validation and minimal target repair. In the analysis phase, the pro-
posed method parses the structure of the project under test through abstract syntax
tree analysis, extracts key methods, dependency relations, and execution paths, and
performs structured rewriting of source code to reduce contextual complexity and
irrelevant information interference. In the generation phase, precise prompts are
constructed based on the structured context to guide the LLM in generating com-
plete test class code. In the validation phase, a dynamic validation mechanism is
proposed to alleviate the “non-impactful omission” problem in traditional validation
workflows by adjusting validation granularity. Meanwhile, a minimal target repair
strategy is introduced by combining automated program repair techniques, enabling
efficient repair with only small code modifications. Experiments are conducted on
four open-source projects, namely Commons-Cli, Commons-Csv, Commons-Lang,
and Gson. The results show that ValiFixTest maintains stable performance in cov-
erage, test pass rate, and test quality metrics. It improves line coverage, mutation
coverage, and the proportion of meaningful assertions on multiple projects, and also
shows good semantic consistency in manual Oracle sampling. The experimental
results indicate that the dynamic validation mechanism and minimal target repair
strategy can reduce invalid generation while improving the executability, assertion
effectiveness, and fault-revealing capability of generated tests.

1 Introduction
Unit testing verifies the smallest independently executable units of software. It can
identify code logic errors and boundary exceptions during development and reduce
later maintenance costs (Dalley 2011). Manually writing and maintaining unit tests
is labor-intensive and time-consuming (Dalley 2011; Mahmud et al. 2025). Studies
have shown that, in medium- and large-scale software projects with more than 500,000
lines of code, the workload of writing unit tests is often substantial, and the time spent
writing test code may even exceed the time spent writing business code (Mahmud
et al. 2025). In addition, human oversight can easily lead to insufficient test coverage.
To address the burden of manual test writing, automated unit testing techniques have
emerged. Their core idea is to directly generate compilable and executable test code
through scripts or specialized tools, thereby improving testing efficiency.
Early automated unit test generation methods mainly focused on search-based, ran-
dom, and symbolic execution techniques. These methods improved testing efficiency to
some extent, but when applied to highly complex software, they still suffered from insuf-
ficient test coverage and poor readability of generated tests (Fraser and Arcuri 2011; Liu
et al. 2024; Cadar et al. 2009; Lukasczyk et al. 2021). In recent years, Large Language
Model (LLM), with strong code understanding and code generation capabilities, have
been widely applied to unit test generation, effectively mitigating many limitations of
traditional methods (Yuan et al. 2024; Chen et al. 2023). However, existing LLM-based
test generation methods still have the following limitations. First, the information used
for generation is static. Prompt construction and focal-context extraction are often fixed
and simplistic, which can lead to context overflow, model hallucination, and insufficient
understanding of test intent (Chen et al. 2023; Feng et al. 2020). Second, validation is
coarse-grained. Relying only on the compiler for exception checking may classify non-
impactful issues as runtime errors, reducing the number of effective tests and degrading
overall coverage (Alagarsamy et al. 2023; Steenhoek et al. 2024).
To address the above problems, this paper proposes an LLM-based automated unit
test generation method iteratively driven by a dynamic validation mechanism and a
minimal target repair strategy, named ValiFixTest. Based on an analysis-generation-
validation framework, the method reconstructs the project under test by identifying
key information, parses core information to generate test code, and uses dynamic
validation and minimal target repair to address insufficient test intent understanding
and coarse-grained validation in the testing process, enabling LLM to better support
unit test generation tasks. The main contributions of this paper are as follows:
1. A structured code analysis and rewriting method for LLM-based test generation is
proposed. It converts raw Java code into a compact context that is more suitable
for LLM understanding. By parsing the structure of the project under test and
extracting key methods, dependency relations, and execution paths, the method
performs unified code reconstruction and context compression on source code,

complexity. It transforms raw code into structured contextual input, allowing the
LLM to more accurately capture core program logic and alleviating insufficient

2. A dynamic validation mechanism and a minimal target repair strategy are pro-
posed. Different from validation-repair workflows that rely only on compilation
feedback or regenerate an entire test class, the proposed method combines rule
validation, logical validation, feasibility validation, and method coverage check-
ing. It dynamically determines the validation scope based on error location, error
type, and validation history, and performs minimal target repair at three granulari-
ties: single-line, method-level, and class-level. This reduces the interference of
irrelevant code during the repair process.
3. Experiments are conducted on open-source projects. The results show that Vali-
FixTest can alleviate invalid generation caused by model hallucination and coarse-
grained validation. Compared with baseline methods, ValiFixTest achieves stable
results in coverage, test pass rate, and test quality metrics. It also shows good test
adequacy and reliability in mutation coverage, proportion of meaningful asser-
tions, fault detection capability, and manual Oracle validation results.
The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces related work. Sec-
tion 3 describes the ValiFixTest method. Section 4 presents the experimental setup,
experimental design, and result analysis. Section 5 discusses limitations and threats
to validity. Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines future work.
2 Related Work
2.1 Traditional Automated Unit Test Generation Methods
Automated unit test generation has undergone several stages of development. Early
research mainly focused on search-based testing, random testing, and symbolic exe-
cution methods (Fraser and Arcuri 2011; Liu et al. 2024; Cadar et al. 2009; Lukas-
czyk et al. 2021; Pacheco and Ernst 2007).
Search-based methods define coverage-oriented objective functions and combine them
with genetic algorithm-based search strategies to iteratively optimize the test space (Abdi
and Mardukhi 2025), thereby effectively exploring the test input space to improve cover-
age. A representative tool is EvoSuite, which uses genetic algorithms to automatically
generate JUnit test cases and continuously optimizes test suites through coverage-driven
fitness functions. It has shown good coverage performance in industrial projects.
Random methods generate test data according to predefined data distribution
rules. They can rapidly produce a large number of test inputs to explore program state
space (Yang et al. 2024) and efficiently detect obvious defects in early testing stages.
For example, Randoop (Pacheco and Ernst 2007) adopts a feedback-directed random
test generation strategy. By continuously expanding the input space through dynamic
execution, it can quickly generate large numbers of test sequences and is efficient in
detecting shallow defects.

Symbolic execution replaces concrete data with symbolic values during program exe-
cution, records path constraints, and solves them to generate test cases, thereby precisely
locating potential problems in complex logic. For example, KLEE (Cadar et al. 2009) and
DART (Sen 2005) systematically explore program paths by combining symbolic execu-
tion with constraint solving, generating test inputs that can reach deep logical branches.
In addition, some studies attempt to combine search strategies with symbolic execu-
tion, such as hybrid concolic testing (Eslamimehr 2026), in which concrete execution and
symbolic execution collaborate to explore program paths and improve path coverage.
However, the design goals of the above traditional methods are mostly limited
to generating test inputs that cover code paths. They are difficult to directly pro-
duce complete unit test code that conforms to testing framework conventions and
has good readability and interpretability (Liu et al. 2024). Meanwhile, when facing
highly complex software systems, traditional methods commonly suffer from insuf-
ficient test coverage and limited practical usefulness of generated results due to path
explosion and large search spaces. Moreover, traditional methods usually lack the
ability to understand program semantic context. The generated test code still has
clear limitations in maintainability and engineering usability, making it difficult to
meet increasingly strict software quality requirements.
2.2 Large Language Model-Driven Generation Methods
With the breakthrough progress of LLM in language understanding and code genera-
tion, a series of LLM-based automated unit test generation techniques have been pro-
posed (Yuan et al. 2024; Chen et al. 2023; Feng et al. 2020), effectively compensating
for the limitations of traditional methods. The success of LLM benefits from pretrain-
ing on large-scale code corpora. LLM can understand program semantics and gen-
erate test code that conforms to testing framework specifications (Feng et al. 2020;
Chen et al. 2021). For example, studies based on Codex and ChatGPT show that
LLM can generate readable test code from function signatures and natural-language
descriptions (Chen et al. 2021). Compared with traditional test generation methods,
LLM can not only generate test inputs, but also automatically supplement assertions,
test structures, and dependency imports, making the generated results closer to manu-
ally written test code (Tufano et al. 2018; Lops et al. 2024). On this basis, researchers
have further proposed a series of LLM-based test generation frameworks optimized
for software engineering scenarios, such as ChatTester (Yuan et al. 2024), ChatUniT-
est (Chen et al. 2023), and HITS (Wang et al. 2024).
ChatTester (Yuan et al. 2024) uses intent prompts to help LLM understand func-
tional logic and generate initial test cases. It then iteratively repairs syntax errors,
missing assertions, and other issues based on error messages and contextual informa-
tion, helping improve the correctness and adequacy of test code.
ChatUniTest (Chen et al. 2023) was the first to propose a generation-validation-
repair closed-loop workflow for LLM. Through an adaptive focal-context generation
mechanism, it precisely extracts key information from target code, drives the model
to generate initial test code, and then uses compiler-based parsing and validation to
guide the model in repairing syntax or compilation errors. Its generated test code
performs well in terms of coverage and readability.

AgoneTest (Lops et al. 2024) focuses on class-level test suite generation. It can
automatically parse Maven/Gradle build files to obtain project dependencies and
Java version information, integrates multidimensional quality assessment tools and
dedicated datasets, supports Java LTS versions, and completes the full test generation
process without manual intervention.
HITS (Wang et al. 2024) introduces method slicing. It decomposes the method under
test into multiple program slices and guides the LLM to generate test code slice by slice,
helping the model more comprehensively cover lines and branches in each slice.
TestART (Gu et al. 2024) was the first to combine automated unit test genera-
tion with APR techniques (Goues et al. 2019). It improves test pass rate and cover-
age through template-based repair and model-assisted repair strategies. For test code
with compilation errors, it first performs automatic repair using templates such as
predefined imports and syntax-error repair patterns. Errors not covered by templates
are then corrected by invoking the LLM. Meanwhile, active prompt injection and
coverage-guided test feedback are used to reduce model hallucination, and the feed-
back is fed into the next generation round (Gu et al. 2024), eventually producing test
code with relatively high pass rate and coverage.
2.3 Generation Methods Based on Software Design Patterns
In addition to search-based, symbolic execution, and LLM-driven methods, test gen-
eration based on software design patterns is also an important direction in automated
testing research. Such methods usually extract test objectives from system architecture,
interface protocols, contract constraints, or object collaboration patterns, and then gen-
erate test inputs and test sequences according to predefined composition rules. Unlike
random generation or coverage-oriented search, design-pattern-based methods empha-
size the use of program structure and interaction relations. Their generated results usu-
ally have clearer test intent and can reduce duplicate and invalid tests to some extent.
In smart contract testing, SmarTS (Gorski 2024) provides a Java package for test suite
generation and execution. It constructs test objectives by using pattern relations among
function calls, state changes, and interaction constraints in smart contracts, and generates
a relatively small test suite through the k+1 method. The core idea of the k+1 method is to
cover k interaction objects or operation combinations and then further add an adjacent or
extended interaction objective, thereby preserving key interaction scenarios while con-
trolling the number of tests. Such methods have the advantages of clear test objectives
and controllable test suite size, and are suitable for software systems with clear contract
interfaces, protocol interactions, and state transition relations.
Design-pattern-based generation methods share a common goal with the pro-
posed method, namely reducing invalid tests through clearer test objectives and
making the generated results focus more on key behaviors. Their main character-
istic is that they first build a test model from relatively stable interface structures,
contract relations, or object collaboration patterns in a domain, and then generate a
small-scale and clearly targeted test suite according to composition rules. Therefore,
such methods have good interpretability and execution efficiency in systems with
explicit smart-contract, protocol-interaction, or state-transition relations. In contrast,
ValiFixTest targets LLM-based unit test generation for general Java projects. It does

not assume that the system under test must have fixed design patterns or domain
contracts. Instead, it automatically extracts test contexts for generation and valida-
tion from ordinary source code through abstract syntax tree (Feng et al. 2020)-based
structural analysis, code rewriting, dynamic validation, and minimal target repair.
In other words, design-pattern-based methods emphasize “generating a minimal test

SmarTS (Gorski 2024) can still provide useful references for future test deduplica-
tion, test objective prioritization, and minimal test set selection in ValiFixTest.
3 ValiFixTest Method
3.1 Overview of the ValiFixTest Framework
ValiFixTest consists of three processes: code analysis for the code under test, test
code generation, and test code validation, as shown in Fig. 1.
After the source code under test is specified, data processing is first performed to
decompose and analyze the structure of the code under test. The code is then uniformly
encoded, reconstructed into a new file, and stored, so as to address possible code smells
and improve code readability. Next, the LLM is used to generate initial test code. After
test generation, the process automatically enters the validation stage, where different
validation objectives are used to ensure test code quality. Specifically, ValiFixTest auto-
matically builds a simulated test execution environment. In this environment, it checks
whether the test code contains issues that affect compilation or execution, marks the
detected issues, and isolates the remaining parts without exceptions. Based on the valida-
tion results, ValiFixTest applies the minimal target repair strategy to capture the marked
range and handle problems within that range in a targeted manner. If the repair is unsuc-
cessful or the repair may affect other code, the repair strategy level is raised. Finally, Vali-
FixTest feeds the processed result back to the simulated environment, and the dynamic
validation mechanism redefines the validation content and validation objective until all

3.2 Test Analysis and Generation
Before test generation begins, it is necessary to fully consider the contextual under-
standing burden that LLM may face when parsing complex code. To reduce the
interference of irrelevant information with model reasoning, ValiFixTest performs
data cleaning and rewriting during the test analysis stage. The cleaning step mainly
removes comments, redundant blank lines, and irrelevant formatting content from
the source code, thereby reducing meaningless textual noise. After cleaning, static
analysis is performed to structurally parse the program under test. An abstract syn-
tax tree (Feng et al. 2020) is used to syntactically parse the source code, and key
structural information closely related to test generation is extracted. Such structural
information includes control-flow structures in target test paths, core method defi-
nitions, method parameter types, return value information, and necessary external
dependency calls. Subsequently, the retained key code structures are normalized and
rewritten according to predefined coding conventions to ensure the conciseness of the
code under test, avoid wasting LLM computation on useless code, and ensure that the
LLM can accurately capture the core functionality and logic of the program. Taking
the code rewriting example in Fig. 2 as an illustration, variable names and method
calls are first standardized to eliminate unnecessarily complex naming structures.
Second, nested control structures are expanded or simplified to make conditional
branches and loop logic clearer. Third, only dependency declarations and method
calls related to the execution path of the target method are retained, while auxil-
iary functions or redundant class members unrelated to test generation are removed.
Finally, the method structure is reorganized according to a unified code formatting
template, including uniform indentation rules, method declaration formats, and
dependency import order. It should be noted that the core structure and functionality
of the code are preserved through another coding representation, and the rewritten
code under test can still clearly express the functional intent.

3.3 Test Validation
The generated test code is submitted to the dynamic validation mechanism for simu-
lated validation. Unlike existing methods that repeatedly execute full validation, the
dynamic validation mechanism provides a virtual test execution environment that can
perform targeted validation based on the error context. The validation process covers
three dimensions: rule validation, logical validation, and feasibility validation. Only
when all of them pass is the test considered successfully generated. When validation
detects an error, the mechanism automatically marks the error location and generates
a complete error report, and then enters the minimal target repair stage. After repair
succeeds, the dynamic validation mechanism focuses only on whether the original
error has been resolved, avoiding full revalidation. If all repair strategies fail or the
maximum number of iterations is reached, the principle of preserving maximum cov-
erage is adopted. The code line or method body containing the error is commented
out or deleted, and executable test methods are retained.

3.3.1 Dynamic Validation Mechanism
The core of the dynamic validation mechanism is to replace traditional one-shot full
validation with hierarchical checking and context-aware validation granularity. Spe-
cifically, rule validation checks the syntactic correctness of test code and ensures
basic constraints such as import paths, type matching, and variable name consistency.
Logical validation simulates test execution paths to verify logical completeness, cov-
ering normal flows, boundary conditions, and exception handling. Feasibility valida-
tion checks the compilability and executability of the code, avoiding test failures
caused by environment mismatch.
When any validation step detects an error, the dynamic validation mechanism
automatically records the error location and type, and generates a structured error
report for repair. After repair is completed, dynamic validation focuses only on the
original error for targeted revalidation, reducing repeated validation overhead. By
taking the code to be validated and the error list to be focused on as input, and out-
putting validation results and an updated error report, this design can alleviate the
“non-impactful omission” problem caused by coarse-grained traditional validation
and make the validation process more targeted. Figure 3 gives an example of the
internal workflow of a virtual test environment.
It should be noted that the proposed dynamic validation mechanism is not a sim-
ple reuse of existing generation-validation-repair workflows. ChatUniTest (Chen et al.
2023) mainly relies on compiler feedback to locate syntax or compilation errors, while
TestART (Gu et al. 2024) relies on the co-evolution of rule templates and coverage feed-
back. In contrast, ValiFixTest further refines the validation object into error-related test
fragments, and integrates rule errors, runtime errors, assertion errors, method coverage
gaps, and validation history into a structured error report. After repair, the system first
verifies whether the original error has been eliminated, and retains test methods that are
unrelated to the error and have already passed validation. This design allows validation
results not only to determine whether test code can run, but also to determine the subse-
quent repair scope and the set of test code that can be retained.

3.3.2 Minimal Target Repair Strategy
The minimal target repair strategy follows the principle of minimal modification. It
determines the minimum repair scope according to error characteristics and selects
the most appropriate RepairAtLevel strategy. The repair strategy is shown in Algo-
rithm 1. Its inputs are the test code to be repaired C, the error report R, and the maxi-
mum number of iterations T. The error list ParseErrors is obtained from the test code
to be repaired by parsing the error report. According to the defect impact scope and
repair granularity, three repair modes are defined: single-line repair (single), method-
level repair (method), and class-level repair (class).
Algorithm 1 Minimal Target Repair Strategy.
In common iterative repair processes, the strategy attempts each repair mode in
sequence. It first adopts the single-line repair mode for isolated errors such as incor-

mode directly corrects the error without affecting other code lines and is the core
of minimal target repair, achieving effective repair benefits with small changes. If
single-line repair cannot solve the problem or introduces new issues, the method-
level repair mode is used. Method-level repair reconstructs or locally rewrites an
entire method when the error involves variable dependencies or multi-line logic. For
changes involving the structure, inheritance relations, interface implementation, or
member variables of the entire class, which usually span multiple methods or even
multiple files, method-level repair is insufficient; therefore, class-level repair is used
to invoke the LLM to regenerate the whole test class or related test methods, achiev-
ing repair through a relatively small scope of regeneration. After each repair attempt,
the dynamic validation mechanism Dynamic Validate is invoked to perform focused
validation on C . The repair result is accepted only when validation passes. If

validation fails, the error list newErrors is updated, the current granularity loop exits,

ensures that partially usable test code can still be output even when some errors can-
not be repaired. At this point, most syntax errors, construction errors, assertion errors,
and runtime errors have already been resolved during single-line repair, method-level
repair, or class-level repair. The fragments that enter PreserveMaxCorrect are usually
a small number of low-value and difficult-to-stabilize fragments. Processing them
prevents a small number of unrepaired code fragments from affecting the output of
the entire test class, thereby improving the usability and completeness of the final
test code.

5 Limitations and Threats to Validity
5.1 Limitations
ValiFixTest improves the executability and test adequacy of LLM-generated unit tests
through structured code rewriting, dynamic validation, and minimal target repair, but
it still has some limitations. First, the method depends on accurate parsing of Java
code structure, build configuration, and testing frameworks. When a project contains
complex reflection, dynamic loading, external service calls, or highly customized
build scripts, abstract syntax tree (Feng et al. 2020) extraction and dependency identi-
fication may not cover all runtime behaviors. Second, dynamic validation may intro-
duce additional invocation costs. Although structured rewriting and minimal target
repair can reduce invalid regeneration, for projects with large dependency sets and
complex failure types, validation content and validation rounds may still increase.
5.2 Threats to Validity
Threats to internal validity mainly come from tool implementation, experimental
scripts, and metric collection. To reduce this risk, this paper runs all methods in a uni-
fied environment, fixes JDK, Maven, JaCoCo, PIT, and model parameters, and repeats
each method six times on each project. Threats to external validity mainly come from
the scope of experimental subjects. This paper selects four Java open-source projects,
Commons-Cli (Apache Commons CLI 2007), Commons-Csv (Apache Commons
CSV 2014), Commons-Lang (Commons 2002), and Gson (Gson 2008), which cover
code with different scales and structures, but they still cannot directly represent all
programming languages, testing frameworks, and industrial closed-source systems.
Threats to construct validity mainly come from whether the selected metrics truly
reflect test quality. Coverage, mutation coverage, assertion density, fault detection
capability, and flaky rate characterize test adequacy from different perspectives, but
no single metric can fully represent test correctness. Therefore, this paper further
introduces manual Oracle sampling to supplement automated metrics in validating
semantic correctness. Threats to conclusion validity mainly come from LLM ran-
domness, prompt sensitivity, and model dependence. This paper fixes the temperature
parameter, repeats runs, reports mean and dispersion results, and uses Mann-Whitney
U tests and Cliff’s Delta to assist in judging the stability of differences. However,
different model versions, prompt templates, and execution times may still affect the
results. Future work will further expand the project scale, introduce more models,
and compare more methods to improve the reproducibility of the conclusions.

6 Conclusion
To address the static information organization and coarse-grained validation problems
in existing LLM-driven automated unit test generation methods, this paper proposes
ValiFixTest, a unit test code generation method driven by dynamic validation and mini-
mal target repair iterations. It keeps unit test generation continuously optimized around
structured context, dynamic feedback, and local repair. Experimental results show that on
the four projects Commons-Cli, Commons-Csv, Commons-Lang, and Gson, ValiFixTest
achieves line coverage values of 79.40%, 66.50%, 78.28%, and 67.15%, respectively,
maintaining stable coverage results on multiple projects. In the test pass-rate experi-
ment, the pass rates of ValiFixTest on the four projects are 70.01%, 54.33%, 52.55%, and
59.56%, respectively, indicating that dynamic validation and minimal target repair can
improve the retention ratio of executable tests. In the test quality evaluation, the mutation
coverage values of ValiFixTest are 48.00%, 45.75%, 58.91%, and 53.22%; the propor-
tions of meaningful assertions are 96.96%, 99.60%, 99.33%, and 99.17%; and the fault
detection capabilities are 79.27%, 70.00%, 69.74%, and 80.99%, respectively. In manual
Oracle sampling, 85.8% of the test methods and their main assertions are consistent with
the expected behavior of the methods under test, with a Cohen’s Kappa value of 0.87.
These results indicate that ValiFixTest can achieve a good balance among cov-
erage scope, executability, assertion effectiveness, and fault-revealing capability on
the selected projects. In the future, this method will be further extended to more
languages and project types. We will also explore integrating ValiFixTest into agent-
based systems, so that analysis, generation, validation, and repair tasks can be col-
laboratively completed by different specialized agents.

C.23 Failure Handling Logic
Failure handling follows the principle of preserving validated correct test content as
much as possible.
PreserveMaxCorrect does not blindly delete failed code. Instead, it uses validation
history to identify the best candidate and preserves, as much as possible, the set of
test methods that can compile, run, and satisfy validation rules.
